snippet.description:
손가락 치켜세우고 호통쳤지만…호랑이 우리 뛰어든 남성 숨져

    (서울=연합뉴스) 영국의 한 동물원에서 시베리아 호랑이 우리에 들어간 남성이 호랑이에게 물려 숨졌습니다.
    텔레그래프 등 현지 매체들에 따르면 10일(현지시간) 낮 영국 동커스터의 요크셔 야생동물공원에서 한 남성이 호랑이 우리 안으로 뛰어들었고 이 남성에게 호랑이 한 마리가 접근해 공격했는데요.
    소셜미디어(SNS)에 유포된 영상을 보면 이 남성은 바닥에 앉은 채로 접근하는 호랑이를 발로 차며 막다가 결국 호랑이에게 목과 가슴 등을 물렸습니다. 
    신고를 받은 응급구조대가 급히 출동했으나 남자는 현장에서 사망 판정을 받았습니다. 
    이 남성의 신원과 호랑이 우리로 들어간 이유는 아직 밝혀지지 않았는데요.
    한 목격자는 "남성이 우리 안으로 뛰어든 뒤 호랑이와 놀려고 했다"고 말했습니다. 자세한 내용은 영상으로 보시죠.

snippet.title: Your Society Has Open Space. But Where Is the Actual Ground? | #architect #landscape #india #cities
snippet.description:
Our parents always told us to walk barefoot on grass. And honestly, I've felt it myself. There's something about walking on actual earth that makes you feel more grounded.

But there's one problem with that advice today. It assumes you have access to the ground.

Most of us live on the fourth floor, the twelfth floor, or the twentieth floor. We've moved upwards, and somewhere along the way, we've lost access to the earth beneath us.

Every housing society claims to have open spaces. And technically, they do.

There's a play area for children, with tiles underneath. Seating for the elderly, surrounded by paved surfaces. And whatever greenery remains is often clipped hedges and ornamental shrubs. It looks green. It looks aesthetic. But there's barely any actual ground where you can walk barefoot, sit under a tree, or let the soil and grass remain undisturbed.

The problem isn't that we don't have open space. It's that we don't have enough living ground.

And the solution isn't necessarily more space. It's using the space we already have differently.

Talk to your RWA about leaving some areas unpaved. Real soil. Real grass. Trees that provide shade and spaces where people can actually sit beneath them.

And if you're buying a home, don't just ask how much open space the society has.

Ask how much of that space is actual ground.

Because green on paper and living ground are two very different things.

I'm Utsav Kamboj, architect and urban designer, documenting How India Builds, the materials, decisions, and stories behind India's built environment.

snippet.title: No Nails, Just Joinery: Watch a Chinese Round-Back Chair Take Shape by Hand
snippet.description:
No nails. No screws. Just wood shaped to lock together.  
Watch a Chinese round-back chair rise from separate pieces in a quiet workshop.  
Stay for the final chair standing alone among the trees.  

This traditional woodworking process follows the making of a Chinese round-back chair. Curved arm pieces, seat panels, legs, and rails are shaped by hand before being joined with mortise-and-tenon construction.

A wooden mallet brings the parts together until the chair finally stands on its own. The finished form is simple, balanced, and built around the beauty of the wood.

Would you keep a chair like this in your home?
